General workflow: in situ imaging-based data

Source: vignettes/general_workflow_insitu.Rmd
general_workflow_insitu.Rmd

In situ imaging-based technologies (MERSCOPE, CosMx, Xenium) detect individual transcripts and segment the cells. The raw data are a table of transcript positions and a set of cell outlines (polygons); expression per cell is obtained by counting the transcripts inside each outline.

This page runs the main steps of a spatial workflow on a small MERSCOPE dataset of the mouse brain (about 80,000 transcripts, 498 cells, 337 genes) from GiottoData. The dataset is small so every step runs in seconds; the results are not meant to be biologically meaningful. The grid workflow runs the same steps on spot-based data. The whole page runs in about 10 seconds with at most 2 GB of memory (Apple M4 Max, one R session).

1 Load the data 

# Install Giotto Suite once (see the Installation page)
install.packages("GiottoUtils",
    repos = c("https://giotto-suite.r-universe.dev", "https://cloud.r-project.org"))
GiottoUtils::suite_install(ref = "disk_full", install_arrow = TRUE)

The mini object already contains processed results. To show the steps from the start, we take its three raw parts, the transcripts, the cell outlines and a DAPI image, and build a new object from them. With your own data, the vendor readers such as importMerscope(), importCosMx() and importXenium() give you the same parts (see import utilities).

library(Giotto)

mini <- GiottoData::loadGiottoMini("vizgen")
transcripts <- getFeatureInfo(mini, feat_type = "rna", return_giottoPoints = TRUE)
cells <- getPolygonInfo(mini, name = "z0", return_giottoPolygon = TRUE)
dapi <- getGiottoImage(mini, name = "dapi_z0")

g <- createGiottoObjectSubcellular(
    gpoints = list(rna = transcripts),
    gpolygons = list(cell = cells),
    images = list(dapi))

spatInSituPlotPoints(g, feats = list(rna = c("Gfap", "Slc17a7", "Olig1", "Cldn5")),
    show_image = TRUE, image_name = "dapi_z0", point_size = 0.4,
    show_polygon = TRUE, polygon_color = "white", polygon_line_size = 0.1)

2 Aggregate transcripts into cells

calculateOverlap() finds the cell outline that contains each transcript, and overlapToMatrix() counts them into a cell by gene expression matrix.

g <- calculateOverlap(g, spatial_info = "cell", feat_info = "rna")
g <- overlapToMatrix(g, poly_info = "cell", feat_info = "rna", name = "raw")

3 Quality control

Besides the detected genes and total counts per cell from addStatistics(), imaging data have two extra checks. The cell area flags segmentation errors, such as fragments a few µm² in size. The Blank- probes are negative controls that measure background; they are removed before analysis.

g <- addStatistics(g, expression_values = "raw")

cell_area <- expanse(getPolygonInfo(g, name = "cell", return_giottoPolygon = TRUE))
g <- addCellMetadata(g, new_metadata = cell_area, by_column = TRUE,
    column_cell_ID = "cell_ID")

spatInSituPlotPoints(g, feats = NULL, show_image = TRUE, image_name = "dapi_z0",
    show_polygon = TRUE, polygon_fill = "total_expr",
    polygon_fill_as_factor = FALSE, polygon_alpha = 0.8,
    polygon_line_size = 0.1)

keep_cells <- pDataDT(g)[area >= 10, cell_ID]
keep_genes <- grep("^Blank-", featIDs(g), value = TRUE, invert = TRUE)
g <- subsetGiotto(g, cell_ids = keep_cells, feat_ids = keep_genes)

g <- filterGiotto(g, expression_threshold = 1, feat_det_in_min_cells = 5,
    min_det_feats_per_cell = 5)

The thresholds are lower than for spot-based data: a gene panel of a few hundred genes detects far fewer genes per cell than whole-transcriptome sequencing does per spot.

4 Normalization 

g <- normalizeGiotto(g)

5 Dimension reduction

Gene panels are designed to contain informative genes, so the PCA uses all of them instead of a highly variable subset (feats_to_use = NULL). With whole transcriptome panels, such as CosMx 6K or Xenium 5K, select highly variable genes first as in the grid workflow.

g <- runPCA(g, feats_to_use = NULL, ncp = 30)

screePlot(g, ncp = 30)

The nearest neighbour network is built first: runUMAP() reuses it for the embedding and doLeidenCluster() clusters on it.

g <- createNearestNetwork(g, type = "kNN", dimensions_to_use = 1:10, k = 15)
g <- runUMAP(g, dimensions_to_use = 1:10, n_neighbors = 15)

6 Clustering 

g <- doLeidenCluster(g, nn_network_to_use = "kNN", network_name = "kNN.pca",
    resolution = 0.5)

plotUMAP(g, cell_color = "leiden_clus", point_size = 2)

With cell outlines, clusters can be shown as filled cells on the image.

spatInSituPlotPoints(g, feats = NULL, show_image = TRUE, image_name = "dapi_z0",
    show_polygon = TRUE, polygon_fill = "leiden_clus",
    polygon_fill_as_factor = TRUE, polygon_alpha = 0.8,
    polygon_line_size = 0.1)

7 Marker genes

findMarkers_one_vs_all() compares each cluster with all other cells. The dot plot shows the top two markers per cluster: dot size is the percentage of cells that express the gene, color the mean expression.

markers <- findMarkers_one_vs_all(g, method = "gini",
    expression_values = "normalized", cluster_column = "leiden_clus",
    min_feats = 5)
top_markers <- markers[, head(.SD, 2), by = "cluster"]

dotPlot(g, feats = unique(top_markers$feats), cluster_column = "leiden_clus")

8 Cell neighbourhoods

At single-cell resolution we can ask which cell types are neighbours more or less often than expected by chance. The spatial network connects each cell to its neighbours; cellProximityMotifs() counts the pairs of neighbouring clusters and compares them with random relabelings of the cells.

g <- createSpatialNetwork(g, method = "Delaunay")

proximities <- cellProximityMotifs(g, spatial_network_name = "Delaunay_network",
    cluster_column = "leiden_clus", size = 2L, n_perm = 1000L)

plotMotifEnrichment(g, proximities)

Pairs to the right of zero (for example 2-2) are neighbours more often than expected, pairs to the left less often. See the Atera breast cancer tutorial for motifs of more than two cells, and interaction changed features for genes whose expression changes next to another cell type.

9 Spatially variable genes

binSpect() works the same way on cells as on spots.

spatial_genes <- binSpect(g)

spatFeatPlot2D(g, feats = spatial_genes$feats[1:4],
    expression_values = "scaled", point_size = 1.5, cow_n_col = 2)

10 Scale up

The same steps run on full slides with hundreds of thousands of cells when the object is stored on disk with GiottoDisk. These tutorials run them on complete datasets:

  • MERSCOPE human colon cancer
  • CosMx human colon, whole transcriptome
  • Xenium human breast cancer

11 Further reading

  • Feature aggregation: how the counts Giotto aggregates from transcripts compare with the vendor’s own cell matrix.
  • Cell type annotation: name the clusters found here.
  • Interaction changed features: genes whose expression in a cell changes next to another cell type.
